intro: Use the clips as a viewing exercise, not as a complete record of a workout. The source is indoor training footage, and the edit selects three shooting sequences; it is not a pickup game and does not show every exercise from the source. The ball trail is a visual overlay, not a measurement of accuracy or mechanics.
heading: Review Three Selected Indoor Shooting Sequences

sections.nav_title: Watch the action before the graphic
sections.heading: Watch the action before the graphic
paragraphs: Play each sequence once at normal speed and follow the real basketball. Notice when the player prepares, releases, and the ball moves toward the basket. On another pass, notice how the tracer draws attention to the flight. Keeping these passes separate makes it easier to describe what is visible without treating the graphic as proof.

sections.nav_title: Write observations that another viewer can check
sections.heading: Write observations that another viewer can check
paragraphs: Use concrete language such as “the ball is visible after release” or “the trail draws my eye toward the rim.” Avoid adding a shot result, distance, player identity, or training outcome unless the footage clearly establishes it. The selected sequences are examples, not a complete sample from which to infer consistency.

sections.nav_title: Turn a viewing pass into a practice note
sections.heading: Turn a viewing pass into a practice note
paragraphs: For your own recording, note which repetition you watched, what remained visible, and what you would need to see again. Keep the original recording available if context before or after a selected clip matters. A short edited video can support a focused question while leaving broader practice evaluation open.
